title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page is Scholion 2, §91 of E449. Euler collects in one table what the paper has established or observed about when ±1, ±2 and ±3 are quadratic residues modulo an odd prime p. He then says the pattern can be extended 'by induction' (that is, empirically), and starts the corresponding tables for ±5. The tables for ±7 and ±11 follow on the next page.

In Legendre-symbol language the table says:
- (−1/p) = 1 if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
- (2/p) = 1 if and only if p ≡ ±1 (mod 8).
- (−2/p) = 1 if and only if p ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8).
- (3/p) = 1 if and only if p ≡ ±1 (mod 12).
- (−3/p) = 1 if and only if p ≡ 1 (mod 3), i.e. p ≡ 1 or −5 (mod 12).
- (5/p) = 1 and (−5/p) = 1 if p ≡ 1 or 9 (mod 20).
- (5/p) = 1 and (−5/p) = −1 if p ≡ −1 or −9 (mod 20).

The page is organised by the class of p modulo 4|a|, with the pair of characters (a/p), (−a/p) given for each class. This is Euler's empirical formulation of the quadratic reciprocity law together with its two supplementary laws: the character of ±a depends only on p mod 4a, with ±1 classes placed symmetrically.

It serves the paper's programme of determining power residues. The preceding pages had proved, by descent arguments on the forms 2pp ± qq, the 'negative' parts of the ±2 cases. The previous page admits that the 'positive' case (±2 residues for p = 8m+1) 'can hardly be shown by similar reasoning'. The next page closes the list with the remark that proofs of these theorems 'would advance the science of numbers not a little'.
errors: None. I checked every entry on this page against the modern Legendre-symbol values: ±1, ±2, ±3 and the first two rows for ±5. All are correct. The ±5, ±7 and ±11 continuations on the next page are also consistent with quadratic reciprocity.
Gap (acknowledged by Euler): only parts of the ±1, ±2, ±3 rows are proved in the paper. The ±5 rows are explicitly inductive conjectures.

ideas.modern_name: First supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on sums of two squares (E241/E228 era), and earlier in E449 itself

ideas.usually_credited_to: Conjectured by Fermat/Euler; proved partly by Lagrange (1775), fully by Gauss (1801)
ideas.where_published: E164 (Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma paa±qbb contentorum); E449 §§87–91

ideas.what: Characters of ±3 by p mod 12, and ±5, ±7, ±11 by p mod 4a, stated by induction
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity law (Euler's conjectural form via residue classes mod 4a)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture); Legendre (1785, incomplete proof); Gauss (1796/1801, proof)
ideas.where_published: E164; E552 (Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos, 1783), where it is stated generally

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's tabular, empirical statement of quadratic reciprocity is well documented (e.g. Weil's Number Theory, Lemmermeyer's Reciprocity Laws, Edwards). This page is one known instance of it, and all entries are correct and standard.
transcription_corrections: 'Erit fi diuifor primus fit' should read 'Erit / si diuisor primus sit'.
'R 2' at the foot is a printer's signature mark, and '+5' is the catchword for the next page; neither is mathematical content.
